Dear GPytorch team,
I am trying to build a model in GPyTorch for inputs of different size (for instance, in the same batch I can have a vector that is, say, 100 elements long, another that is 56 elements long, and another that is 29 elements long). This would be a generalization of having interdomain inducing points, i.e. inducing points with size different from the datapoints. However, in my case, the datapoints themselves can also be of different size.
Do you have any recommendations on how to implement a model like this? I find three main difficulties:


From what I understand, GPyTorch kernels register and remember the input size (probably they register it when they are first called?) and they complain if subsequent inputs are of different size. I think that I could bypass this by padding the smaller inputs with 0's, making a note of the real size of each input, and passing that information to the kernel, so that all the padding is ignored.

I guess I should write my own version of VariationalStrategy?


Pytorch doesn't have ragged tensors, so implementing a vectorized version of the kernel will be daunting. This problem is inherent to Pytorch and not GPyTorch, but any thoughts would be greatly appreciated!

🚀 Feature Request
Add support for batched SKI kernel approximations. I'm not sure how one would go about adding this functionality. Ideally GridInterpolationKernel would infer the batch shape from base_kernel.
If this can't be done soon, we should add a warning that GridInterpolationKernel doesn't support batch evaluation. Currently it seems to fail silently by producing incorrectly shaped outputs.
>>> import torch
>>> import gpytorch
>>> base_kernel = gpytorch.kernels.RBFKernel(batch_shape=torch.Size([2]))
>>> ski_kernel = gpytorch.kernels.GridInterpolationKernel(base_kernel, num_dims=1, grid_size=128)
>>> a = torch.rand(2)
>>> ski_kernel(a, a).shape
torch.Size([2, 2])
>>> base_kernel(a, a).shape
torch.Size([2, 2, 2])

Motivation
In general for multi-dimensional outputs we have to train and evaluate multiple GPs in parallel. Currently this functionality appears to be completely absent in GridInterpolationKernel. I think SKI could have compelling applications in the context of online model learning, where one may be unable or unwilling to solve a slowly converging variational optimization problem.
Pitch
Ultimately it would be amazing if batch_shape could be added as an argument to the GridInterpolationKernel constructor, or inferred from the base kernel. I'm not sure how much work this would involve.
One alternative could be relying on a multitask-like approach, but this requires memory usage that scales quadratically with the output dimension, which quickly becomes impractical.
I'd be willing to open a pull request, but I'd need some pointers for how to get started. How was arbitrary batch_shape supported in the first place?

As in page 4 of Gardner et al, 2018, suppose I want to estimate the trace of

Hi All,
I am trying to build models for doing multi-task regression and have some key questions about speed at prediction time for these models. I'm looking for intuition from you all on why two seemingly similar models run at very different speeds.
In my application, not all tasks appear together; I therefore need capabilities like the Hadamard_multitask_gp_regression example notebook.  FYI, I'm also using the multitask_fantasies branch with a relatively recent version of master merged into it.
On to my specifics:
I have two model classes, A and B, both derived from gpytorch.models.ExactGP. In each case, the input to the kernels is run through (very similar) shallow neural networks to do some feature transformation (removed from the examples below).
Model class A has a kernel defined like so in its init method:
self.covar_module = gpytorch.kernels.RBFKernel()
self.task_covar_module = gpytorch.kernels.IndexKernel(
                num_tasks=num_tasks, rank=num_tasks-1)

and a forward method in which
def forward(self, x, i):
...
covar_x = self.covar_module(x)
covar_i = self.task_covar_module(i)
covar = covar_x.mul(covar_i)
return gpytorch.distributions.MultivariateNormal(mean_x, covar)

where mean_x is defined via the model's mean_module.
Similarly, B has the a kernel defined as follows in init:
self.covar_module = \
                gpytorch.kernels.RBFKernel(
                    active_dims=torch.tensor(stationary_dims)
                ) +\
                gpytorch.kernels.LinearKernel(
                    active_dims=torch.tensor(linear_dims)
                )

self.task_covar_module = gpytorch.kernels.IndexKernel(
                num_tasks=num_tasks, rank=num_tasks-1)

where stationary_dims and linear_dims split the (expanded) feature dimension, and a forward method:
def forward(self, x, i):
...
xall = torch.cat([xstationary, xlin], dim=1)
covar_x = self.covar_module(xall)
covar_i = self.task_covar_module(i)
covar = covar_x.mul(covar_i)
return gpytorch.distributions.MultivariateNormal(mean_x, covar)

At prediction time, the model has training data from O(10k) observations and is given a set of O(10k) targets (feature vectors pred_x and indices pred_i). I'm computing a single, big ol' multivariate normal over all of the targets, where I'm doing it as follows:
with torch.no_grad(), gpytorch.settings.fast_pred_var(), gpytorch.settings.max_root_decomposition_size(1e5):
        joint_mvn = model(pred_x, pred_i)

The max_root_decomposition_size is enormous and does make this already take a long time.  It's necessary because I care quite a lot about the fine, across-task structure of the posterior, which (as far as I've been able to tell) tends to be resolved poorly with the default value.
The weird thing is that, when applied at prediction time, model B (with the additive kernel) takes MUCH longer to run. I unfortunately don't have access to exact timings at the moment, but model class A makes predictions in seconds in this setting, whereas model class B takes 15+ minutes.  The only thing that seems plausible to me is that this is related to the additive structure of the kernel; it does seem odd that this is not optimized, however.  I have noticed some similar problems with the product structure of the spatial and task covariance, which is part of what's led me to do a single, big covariance calculation (that's a different story).
Do any of you have intuition as to why model class B takes so much longer to predict than A does?
